title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F08
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 40 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for the narrative on the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires. Identify the affected study area, select an appropriate Earth observation dataset for mapping burn scars, retrieve data covering the region, and explain why the chosen dataset is suitable and how it relates to the narrative.

answers.text:
The narrative from the EO Dashboard identifies the affected study area as southeast Australia, where approximately 74,000 sq km of eucalyptus forest were impacted during the 2019–2020 bushfire season.

While the narrative specifically emphasizes the use of Copernicus Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI) for measuring atmospheric emissions (CO, $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{SO}_2$) to quantify the 700 million metric tons of $\text{CO}_2$ released, these datasets are not suitable for mapping the physical burn scars on the ground. For that purpose, Sentinel-2 is the most appropriate dataset because its multi-spectral optical imagery allows for the identification of charred vegetation and the calculation of burn indices (like NBR).

I have retrieved a Sentinel-2 quicklook image of the region for visual inspection:
sentinel2_20260807T092924_68df81.jpg

Summary of Suitability:
• Sentinel-5P (Narrative focus): Suitable for atmospheric monitoring and emission quantification (the "why" of the climate impact).
• Sentinel-2 (Mapping focus): Suitable for spatial delineation of burn scars due to high spatial resolution and spectral bands sensitive to vegetation health and charcoal.

Final Summary and Results

1. EO Dashboard Narrative Details
The 2019–2020 Australian bushfires narrative from the EO Dashboard provides the following key insights:
• Study Area: Southeast Australia, including regions like New South Wales, Victoria, and parts of South Australia.
• Total Area Burned: ~74,000 sq km of eucalyptus forest, with fires releasing 700 million metric tons of CO₂.
• Key Datasets: Tropomi instrument on Copernicus Sentinel-5P (for atmospheric emissions like CO, NO₂, and SO₂).
• Purpose: The narrative emphasizes the atmospheric impact of the fires, but burn scar mapping requires high-resolution optical or multispectral data (e.g., Sentinel-2).

2. Dataset Selection for Burn Scar Mapping
Sentinel-2 L2A (Surface Reflectance) was selected for burn scar mapping because:
• High Spatial Resolution: 10m–60m (depending on band), ideal for detecting fine-scale burn scars.
• Surface Reflectance: L2A products are atmospherically corrected, making them suitable for time-series analysis (e.g., pre- and post-fire comparisons).
• Spectral Bands:
  • B04 (Red, 665nm): Sensitive to vegetation health and burn severity.
  • B08 (NIR, 842nm): Highlights vegetation density (low reflectance post-fire).
  • B12 (SWIR, 2190nm): Penetrates smoke and detects moisture stress (burn scars appear bright).
• Indices for Burn Scars:
  • Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR): (NIR - SWIR) / (NIR + SWIR) — ideal for burn severity mapping.
  • NDVI: (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) — useful for vegetation loss detection.

3. Retrieved Data
• Source: Google Earth Engine (GEE) was used to retrieve Sentinel-2 L2A data for the period October 1, 2019 to March 31, 2020.
• Bounding Box: [140.0, -38.0, 155.0, -28.0] (covers southeast Australia).
• Output: 20 GeoTIFF files (surface reflectance) for bands B04, B08, and B12, located at:

  gee_image_20191001_t1_n1_q1.tif
  gee_image_20191001_t1_n2_q1.tif
  ...
  gee_image_20191007_t4_n3_q1.tif

4. Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) Calculation
• Process:
  1. Concatenated the Sentinel-2 L2A bands (B04, B08, B12) into a single multi-band raster.
  2. Computed the NBR using the formula:
     \[
     \text{NBR} = \frac{\text{B08} - \text{B12}}{\text{B08} + \text{B12}}
     \]
  3. Clipped the result to the bounding box [140.0, -38.0, 155.0, -28.0].
• Output: The final NBR raster is saved as a single-band GeoTIFF at:

  nbr_clipped.tif

5. Why This Dataset is Suitable
• Temporal Coverage: The dataset spans the peak fire period (October 2019–March 2020), allowing for pre- and post-fire comparisons.
• Spatial Coverage: Covers the entire southeast Australia region, including the most affected areas.
• Quantitative Use: The NBR output enables GIS analysis (

Based on the retrieved Sentinel-2 true-color imagery for southeast Australia covering January 2020, here is the analysis:

Affected Study Area
The affected study area identified from the EO Dashboard narrative is southeast Australia, specifically encompassing regions such as New South Wales and Victoria. The imagery covers a bounding box of 135.0, -38.0, 155.0, -28.0, which aligns with the geographic extent of the 2019–2020 bushfires.

Selected Earth Observation Dataset
The chosen dataset for mapping burn scars is Sentinel-2 L2A true-color imagery. This dataset is suitable for the following reasons:

1. High Spatial Resolution: Sentinel-2 provides a spatial resolution of 10–60 meters, which is sufficient to detect and map burn scars at a fine scale, especially in areas with significant vegetation cover like eucalyptus forests.

2. True-Color Imagery: The true-color band combination (B04, B03, B02) allows for visual interpretation of land cover changes, making it ideal for identifying burn scars through color contrast between burned and unburned areas.

3. Temporal Coverage: The imagery from January 2020 captures the aftermath of the bushfires, allowing for the visualization of burn scars and their extent.

4. Open Access and Consistency: Sentinel-2 data is freely available and processed to Level 2A, which corrects for atmospheric effects and provides a consistent baseline for comparison across different time periods.

Relation to the Narrative
The Sentinel-2 imagery directly relates to the narrative by providing a visual representation of the affected areas. The narrative highlights that the fires burned approximately 74,000 square kilometers of eucalyptus forest in southeast Australia. The imagery allows for the identification and mapping of these burned areas, offering a spatial context to the narrative's quantitative data on emissions and affected regions.

In summary, the Sentinel-2 L2A true-color imagery is an appropriate dataset for mapping burn scars in the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires due to its high resolution, true-color capability, and temporal relevance. It complements the narrative by providing a visual confirmation of the extent and impact of the fires.

The Sentinel-2 Level-2A data for southeast Australia during the 2019–2020 bushfires has been successfully retrieved and analyzed. The image, which includes bands 4 (red), 3 (green), 2 (blue), and 12 (shortwave infrared), clearly shows burn scars as areas of reddish-brown and gray tones, contrasting with the green vegetation that remains unaffected. This data is suitable for burn scar analysis because it includes Band 12 (SWIR), which is critical for detecting burned areas due to its sensitivity to changes in vegetation moisture and surface reflectance post-fire.

The chosen dataset is appropriate for the narrative on the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires because:
1. It covers the affected study area (southeast Australia) during the critical fire period (December 2019 to February 2020).
2. It provides the necessary spectral bands (including SWIR) to calculate the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR), which is a standard index for identifying and mapping burn scars.
3. The data is at Level-2A, meaning it has been atmospherically corrected and is ready for analysis, ensuring accurate and reliable results.

The NBR calculation, using Band 8 (NIR) and Band 12 (SWIR), would highlight the burned areas as they exhibit a significant decrease in NIR reflectance and an increase in SWIR reflectance after a fire. This would allow for the generation of a detailed map of the burn scars, providing valuable insights into the extent and severity of the bushfires as described in the narrative.

items.question: What MSG SEVIRI product variants are available on the EUMETSAT server and what satpy reader should be used to open them?

answers.text:
Here are the MSG SEVIRI product variants available on the EUMETSAT server, along with the corresponding satpy reader to use for opening them:

MSG SEVIRI Product Variants
Product Key               | Product ID                     | Satpy Reader       | Available BandsMSG-SEVIRI-L1-HRY           | EO:EUM:DAT:MSG:HRSEVIRI          | seviri_l1b_hrit      | VIS006, VIS008, IR_016, IR_039, WV_062, WV_073, IR_087, IR_097, IR_108, IR_120, IR_134, HRV
MSG-SEVIRI-L1-IODC          | EO:EUM:DAT:MSG:HRSEVIRI-IODC     | seviri_l1b_hrit      | VIS006, VIS008, IR_016, IR_039, WV_062, WV_073, IR_087, IR_097, IR_108, IR_120, IR_134, HRV
MSG-SEVIRI-RSS              | EO:EUM:DAT:MSG:MSG15-RSS         | seviri_l1b_hrit      | VIS006, VIS008, IR_016, IR_039, WV_062, WV_073, IR_087, IR_097, IR_108, IR_120, IR_134
Notes:
1. Satpy Reader: All MSG SEVIRI products use the seviri_l1b_hrit satpy reader.
2. Bands:
   • HRV refers to the High-Resolution Visible channel.
   • The other bands follow the standard SEVIRI channel naming convention (e.g., VIS006 for visible channel at 0.6 µm, IR_108 for infrared channel at 10.8 µm).
3. Product Types:
   • MSG-SEVIRI-L1-HRY: Standard SEVIRI Level 1.5 HRIT format.
   • MSG-SEVIRI-L1-IODC: SEVIRI Level 1.5 HRIT format for the Indian Ocean Data Coverage (IODC) service.
   • MSG-SEVIRI-RSS: Rapid Scanning Service (RSS) data, providing higher temporal resolution for specific regions.

     • VIS006, VIS008
     • IR_016, IR_039

All MSG SEVIRI products use the same satpy reader (seviri_l1b_hrit) for opening the downloaded files.

Notes:
1. Satpy Reader: All MSG SEVIRI products use the seviri_l1b_hrit satpy reader.
2. Bands:

   • The other bands follow the standard SEVIRI channel naming convention (e.g., VIS006 for visible channel at 0.6 µm, IR_108 for infrared channel at 10.8 µm).

answers.text:
The hourly ERA5 data for total column water vapour for January 2023 over Central Europe has been downloaded to:
tcwv_hourly_2023_01.nc

Unfortunately, the automated temporal aggregation tools in the climate sub-agent failed due to a coordinate naming mismatch (valid_time vs time), and the GIS analysis server is currently optimized for GeoTIFFs rather than NetCDF temporal aggregation.

To obtain the monthly mean field, you can use the following Python snippet with xarray:

import xarray as xr

Load the dataset
ds = xr.open_dataset('tcwv_hourly_2023_01.nc')

Calculate the monthly mean across the 'valid_time' dimension
monthly_mean = ds['tcwv'].mean(dim='valid_time')

Save the result
monthly_mean.to_netcdf('tcwv_monthly_mean_2023_01.nc')
